explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, letters AND a gift. Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent both to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:12). Getting mail with a present attached is a good day for anybody. I'd open that one first.

No warning came in this mail, baker. The text says Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift (2 Kings 20:12). The warning shows up later, and it comes from Isaiah the prophet, not from Babylon. This envoy showed up with a present, not bad news.

A summons would be a royal "come here right now" note, and that's not what arrived. Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift (2 Kings 20:12). Nobody got ordered anywhere. Nobody opens a gift hoping it's a court date, friend.

explanations.answer: He heard Hezekiah had been ill
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, baker. Merodach-baladan sent letters and a gift "for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness." (2 Kings 20:12) Word travels, even to a distant land. Nothing else is listed as the cause.

explanations.answer: Hezekiah had sent him gifts first
explanations.explanation: The text never says Hezekiah sent anything first, baker. It says Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent his letters and gift because "he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness." (2 Kings 20:12) Nobody is keeping a gift scoreboard here. The reason is the illness.

explanations.answer: He wanted to start trading with Judah
explanations.explanation: Trading is a fine idea, but it's not what the text says. The reason given is that the king of Babylon "had heard about Hezekiah’s illness." (2 Kings 20:12) I'd be guessing if I said more, and I try not to guess about reasons. I stick to what the verse gives.

explanations.answer: Everything in his palace and kingdom
explanations.explanation: EVERYTHING, baker. The text says "There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them." (2 Kings 20:13) Silver, gold, spices, oil, armory, storehouses, the whole lot. That's a tour with no skipped rooms.

explanations.answer: Only what was in his treasure house
explanations.explanation: The treasure house was just one stop, friend. Hezekiah also showed them his armory and all that was in his storehouses (2 Kings 20:13). The verse says "There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them." That's a lot more than one room.

explanations.answer: Only the rooms his guests asked to see
explanations.explanation: The text never says the guests asked for anything, baker. It says Hezekiah showed them "all that was found in his storehouses." (2 Kings 20:13) He was the one giving this tour. Nobody had to ask, and nothing was held back.
True, baker. The armory is right there in the list: "as well as his armory." (2 Kings 20:13) Silver, gold, spices, oil, and the place where the weapons were kept. He showed them all of it.

This one is true, baker. The text says Hezekiah showed the envoys "the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his armory." (2 Kings 20:13) The armory made the tour. He left nothing out.

Not quite, baker. Hezekiah says the envoys "came from a distant land," and then names it: "from Babylon." (2 Kings 20:14) Distant, not nearby. Isaiah asked where they came from, and the king answered plainly.
False is right, baker. Hezekiah answers Isaiah, "They came from a distant land… from Babylon." (2 Kings 20:14) Close by it was not. Isaiah asked a direct question and he got a direct answer.

The text says the opposite, baker. Isaiah gives the LORD's word: "everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD." (2 Kings 20:17) Not a few things. Nothing.

False is right, baker. The LORD says everything in the palace and all that Hezekiah's fathers had stored up will be carried off to Babylon, and then He says, "Nothing will be left." (2 Kings 20:17) Not a few left behind, and not a single cookie crumb of treasure.

Babylon, baker. The same place those envoys came from. The LORD says everything in the palace "will be carried off to Babylon." (2 Kings 20:17) The visitors had seen it all, and now Isaiah says where it's going.

Assyria is a fair guess, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says everything in the palace "will be carried off to Babylon." (2 Kings 20:17) That's the land the envoys had just come from, the distant one.

Egypt isn't the answer here, friend. The word of the LORD says everything in the palace "will be carried off to Babylon." (2 Kings 20:17) Same Babylon that sent the letters and the gift. The envoys had just seen the whole place.

Descendants, baker. Isaiah says, "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." (2 Kings 20:18) I think this is the heavy part of the word. It's not only about treasure anymore.

Soldiers aren't mentioned here, baker. Isaiah says "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away." (2 Kings 20:18) This is a family word. I think it hits harder than a list of treasures.

Not servants, friend. Isaiah says it's "some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood" who will be taken away to the palace of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 20:18). That's Hezekiah's own family line. I think that's why this part of the word is so heavy.

explanations.answer: The word of the LORD is good
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, baker. Hezekiah answers Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (2 Kings 20:19) It's a surprising thing to say right after hearing that. The next verse tells us what he was thinking.

explanations.answer: Ask the LORD to spare my family
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show him asking for that, baker. Hezekiah says, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (2 Kings 20:19) No plea, no bargaining. Just that one line, and then the verse tells us what he was thinking.

explanations.answer: This word is too heavy to bear
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick it, baker, because it IS a heavy word. But Hezekiah doesn't say that. He says, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (2 Kings 20:19) That's his whole reply to Isaiah.

explanations.answer: There will be peace in his lifetime
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says, "For he thought, 'Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?'" (2 Kings 20:19) That's the thought behind his words. Only he knows what he was feeling inside.

explanations.answer: The LORD will change His mind
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. It says Hezekiah thought, "Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?" (2 Kings 20:19) That's the thought the verse gives us. Nothing in it says he expected the word to change.

explanations.answer: His sons will win the treasure back
explanations.explanation: No, friend, that thought isn't in the verse. It says Hezekiah thought, "Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?" (2 Kings 20:19) His mind was on his own days, and nothing about his sons winning anything back.

True, baker. The verse says Hezekiah "constructed the pool and the tunnel to bring water into the city." (2 Kings 20:20) A pool and a tunnel. That's a lot of digging, and I'd have needed a very long mustache.

This one is true, baker. The text says Hezekiah "constructed the pool and the tunnel to bring water into the city." (2 Kings 20:20) It's one of the things written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. He built it, and it carried water.
Manasseh, baker. "His son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Kings 20:21) Hezekiah rested with his fathers, and the throne passed to his son. That wraps up the story of Hezekiah.

Josiah is a name from the kings of Judah, but it's not the one here, baker. The verse says, "his son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Kings 20:21) Manasseh is the son who takes the throne after Hezekiah.

Jotham is another king of Judah, friend, but he isn't Hezekiah's son in this verse. It says, "his son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Kings 20:21) Manasseh took the throne after Hezekiah rested with his fathers.
